catalog_quote: [ch.4, p.12] Specifically, heavy syllables in Hidatsa include any long vowel, diphthong or any syllable that carries a coda. ... However, I show here that metrical prominence in Hidatsa is unpredictable because accent [´] in a word, which always coincides with high tone (H), (henceforth F0) may or may not coincide with the default stress, which lands on an iambic foot that is aligned with the left edge of a word (L´L), (L´H) or (´H). [ch.2, p.4, quoting Boyle et al. 2016] Boyle et al. stated that “primary stress is predictable and falls on the second syllable unless the initial syllable is heavy (i.e., (C)VV, (C)Vh, (C)Vʔ) or the third syllable is heavy and the first two are light” (Boyle et al., 2016). [ch.5, p.15] Of the 861 roots, 779 fell into the default class, Class I (Iambic), 32 fell into Class II (Accent on the initial mora of a word, which is a light syllable), 39 fell into Class III (Accent on the first mora to the right of the initial iamb), and 10 fell into neither class because the words either included an indefinite marker /maa-/ or the prefix /naga/ ‘by sudden motion or inner force’.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Hidatsa is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title, Rivera 2017 (CSU Fresno MA thesis), was already held by the project with a text and was re-read in full: it gives an explicit, corpus-based placement statement (pp.12-15) -- default accent on a left-aligned weight-sensitive iamb (´H / L´H / L´L), 779/861 trisyllabic roots, with lexical exceptions (32 initial-light, 39 post-iamb) -- plus instrumental results (pp.20-27) showing F0 and amplitude mark one accented mora per word with no leftward pitch spread (contra Park 2012). Boyle et al. 2024 (held by the project) and Kasak 2024 fn.47-48 (held by the project) agree on quantity-sensitive left-edge iambic stress. Still unobtained: Boyle et al. 2016 SSILA paper (source of the 'second syllable unless initial heavy' rule; high), Metzler 2021 CSU Fresno MA thesis (high), Park 2012 IU dissertation (ProQuest; medium). The CORE download URL for Rivera now returns HTTP 400 and the CORE/ScholarWorks landing pages could not be reached by automated download; the CORE API record (work 294194707, OAI oai:scholarworks:6m311q860) was saved and updated.

new_statements.rule_in_words: One prominent (high-F0, higher-amplitude) syllable per word. Default site is a left-aligned quantity-sensitive iamb: the second syllable if the first is light (CV/V), the first syllable if it is heavy (long vowel, diphthong or coda); ~90% of trisyllabic roots follow this. A lexical minority carries accent on an initial light syllable or on the mora immediately after the initial iamb. Boyle et al. 2016 (quoted p.4) state the same default as 'second syllable unless the initial syllable is heavy, or the third syllable is heavy and the first two are light'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated by Rivera; Stetson 1946 mentions in passing 'secondary stress of a long compound breath group'.
new_statements.exceptions: 82 of 861 roots non-default: Class II accent on an initial light syllable (e.g. gírashi 'to love', áwashi 'cave'), Class III accent on the mora right of the initial iamb (agshí 'to catch', garawí 'to remember', adarúu 'to get hurt'), one HLH́ item (ookacía 'to soar'); words with indefinite maa- or prefix naga- excluded. Rivera's own weight criterion counts every coda as moraic, whereas Boyle et al. 2016 count only (C)VV, (C)Vh, (C)Vʔ as heavy.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation forms: trisyllabic noun and verb roots from the Boyle & Gwin 6000-word dictionary recordings (three fluent speakers, words in isolation, 2015-16). Analyses conflict in the literature: Park 2012 (reference grammar) = lexical pitch accent with leftward H spread; Boyle et al. 2016/2024, Metzler 2021, Kasak 2024 = predictable quantity-sensitive left-aligned iambic stress; Rivera = default iamb plus lexical classes, cued by F0 ('pitch accent' phonetically) with no spread.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Hidatsa (hida1246, ISO hid) as spoken on the Fort Berthold Reservation, North Dakota; Rivera's data are three fluent speakers recorded 2015-16 plus The Language Conservancy dictionary recordings; no dialect differentiation is made. Not to be confused with Gros Ventre/Atsina (Algonquian), an old alternative name for the Hidatsa.

new_statements.quote: p.12: "the default stress, which lands on an iambic foot that is aligned with the left edge of a word (L´L), (L´H) or (´H)". p.13: "The majority of the words fell into the default category (iambic-´H, L´H, L´L) where accent is placed on the left-aligning iamb in a word. However, accent [´] is found in other places as well; these include on the initial mora in a word where a light syllable is, on the first mora to the right of an initial iamb (regardless of syllable weight), and on the last mora of a word." p.15: "Of the 861 roots, 779 fell into the default class, Class I (Iambic), 32 fell into Class II ..., 39 fell into Class III ..., and 10 fell into neither class"
new_statements.citation: Rivera, Amanda Leigh (2017). Metrical prominence in Hidatsa: an acoustic and phonological analysis. MA thesis, California State University, Fresno, pp.12-15.
new_statements.reading: Word accent in Hidatsa is, by default, a left-aligned weight-sensitive iamb: the initial syllable if heavy (long vowel, diphthong or coda), otherwise the second syllable regardless of its weight. This holds for 779 of 861 trisyllabic dictionary roots (90.5%); the remainder is a lexical residue (32 with accent on a light initial syllable, 39 with accent on the syllable right after the initial iamb, 11 other). Equivalent to Boyle et al. 2016's rule 'second syllable unless the initial is heavy (or the third is heavy after two lights)'. Phonetically the accented mora carries higher F0 and amplitude (not duration), one per word, with no pitch spread; Rivera calls this a pitch accent, Boyle et al. 2024 and Kasak 2024 call it quantity-sensitive stress. For a catalog entry: fixed/predictable weight-sensitive left-edge (initial-if-heavy, else peninitial) with ~9% lexical exceptions.

tone_statements.quote: Further evidence against asymmetrical iambs comes from Hidatsa. Hidatsa has left-aligning QS iambs (Boyle et al. 2016, Metzler 2017) and intervocalic voicing of stops and affricates (Harris & Voegelin 1939: 183). Intervocalic voicing in Hidatsa is gradient and governed by foot position; intervocalic voicing is most prominent foot-medially, less so foot-initially, and least in unparsed syllables (Driscoll & Metzler 2018).

sources.quote: sec.2.3: "Harris and Voegelin (in Lowie 1939), Robinett (1954, 1955), Jones (1978) and Boyle (2007) all argue that it is lexical. Park (2012) proposes that Hidatsa has a pitch accent system similar to Crow. Rivera (2017) and Metzler (2021) have shown Park's claims to be erroneous. In this study, we noted that in each word there is one syllable that is prominent (i.e., what we term stress)." sec.4: "One interesting finding from this study is that long vowels tend to attract stress ... it is consistent with Metzler (2021) in that Hidatsa has a quantitate [sic] sensitive stress pattern."
